[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.

review_text_raw:
This game is currently in the Humble Bundle for April 2021. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 4th, 2021, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

After an playing an hour of Simulacra and Simulacra 2 to review for the Humble Choice April 2021 Bundle:

These are a pair of horror or thriller games.  The first game spooked me with a major opening that has a lot of horror elements in it, but then didn’t do much with the horror aspect in the next 40 minutes.  Instead, it focused more on what life would be like as a woman.

Simulacra has you find a woman’s phone and then try to figure out what happened to her.  Though while playing it I noticed how freaking awful it would be to be a woman.  There’s a solid social commentary on how some people spoke to the mystery girl online and it’s done in a very strong way.  This isn’t social commentary being forced in there, but instead a strong point the game makes. 

The gameplay is mostly about snooping on the phone and has voyeuristic qualities to it.  You can even impersonate her with different people, and it’s quite interesting.  As much as I dislike the horror aspect in the beginning because I’m a scaredy-cat, I found myself wanting to play more as it’s more of a thriller.

Simulacra 2 seems to up the production values but presents a very similar experience.  Though I do want to mention there are a few grammar issues that I noticed in both games, and apparently, the team who created the game is from Malaysia, which might explain that.  Nothing that bad, but it can be a bit noticeable. 

Pick this up if you like horror or thriller, these aren’t long games, but they are unique.  There are some effective and interesting moments, such as hearing a woman’s voice from behind you if you’re playing wearing headphones. 

If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my youtube channel:

https://youtu.be/KQoCrsCpfF0

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good.

review_text_raw:
I am generally biased to be forgiving of FMV interactive movies, so of course I've played others like Her Story, #WarGames, The Bunker, Late Shift, and The Shapeshifting Detective.  Like those games, this game is relatively short on total content, with moments of good acting and then...well, near-miss moments that make you cringe.  Also, these games tend to have multiple achievements and scenes that you can't get in one playthrough, which is a way of extending the replay value, but I seldom feel particularly inclined to watch the repeated parts over and over again.

This game is unique due to the phone interface and the clever design that it took to make that work.  You feel like it really could be you deciding what to do in this situation, but then sometimes you're reminded how you can't actually do anything like answer a phone call.  So when it works, it's great, but it has built-in limitations to just how far the concept can go.  I commend them for the creepy story.  I wish the really uneven voice acting hadn't pulled me out of it from time to time.  At least Anna (whose phone you've found) is done consistently well.

Your first full playthrough will take 3-4 hours depending on how much you read, and subsequent plays should take you a bit less.  Alternate achievements, videos, conversations, and endings are basically earned by the responses you choose, like who to be nice to, who to scold, and who to trust.  The downside of that is like the decisions in Telltale games, especially The Walking Dead: you'll have to replay with lots of choices that you'd never make in real life if you want to see the other paths.  In that regard, replays are more like gaming the game and less like experiencing the story.  But overall, that's a complaint that's bound to be true of every choose-your-own-adventure game you can find.  So you know what you're getting.  If you like that, and you have a tolerance for FMV games, this one is certainly worth $5.

The downside of that is like the decisions in Telltale games, especially The Walking Dead: you'll have to replay with lots of choices that you'd never make in real life if you want to see the other paths. In that regard, replays are more like gaming the game and less like experiencing the story. But overall, that's a complaint that's bound to be true of every choose-your-own-adventure game you can find. So you know what you're getting. If you like that, and you have a tolerance for FMV games, this one is certainly worth $5.

Simulacra is a "found phone" psychological mystery / horror game where your curiosity has gotten you involved with a mystery... You found this phone on your doorstep. You initially have no idea what to enter, then the phone glitched and revealed its passcode. You find chat logs, call logs, and the owner was Anna. There was a corrupted video where a terrified Anna screamed that don't come after her... Then the message was cut off. 

As you scan the phone's various steps for clues, and maybe even engage in some social engineering with Anna's friends, including (ex-?) boyfriend Greg, bestie Ashley, and dating app date Taylor, you need to reconstruct Anna's life before she went missing, to have a chance at finding out what happened to her...  

The videos are very high quality, but the simulated phone calls don't sound nearly as good. 

The special effects where the phone glitched got the definitely horror feel to it. Same with the time-warp feel when the phone really glitches out. 

The puzzles such as the sentence scramble and photo scramble doesn't quite fit into the gameplay though.  The "sentence scramble" feels a bit of "make work". Same with the photo scramble. 

There seems to be a lot of alternative paths one can take, so there would be a lot of additional achievements should you want a replay or two. 

All puzzles have clues accessible within the phone itself, though some may be more obscure than others. Part of the fun is to figure out the rest. And there are a lot of red herrings. 

All in all, interesting mechanic for a puzzle game and gradual revelation, if you dig this sort of game.

review_text_raw:
Fun little puzzle/"hacking" simulator with creepy supernatural elements. The dialogue is a bit sloppy, and the voice acting is laughably bad, but the storyline is engaging enough for multiple playthroughs. Gameplay is fairly standard for these sorts of games (not a bad thing), and character interactions seem natural enough to maintain immersion.

Don't expect much in the way of a challenge, though; the emphasis is definitely more on the progression of the story and the character interactions. The puzzles (and I'm using the word loosely here) consist of very simple "decrypting" of texts and photos, as well as base-tier social engineering to suss out key bits of information (to be used to unlock accounts, etc). You'll want to keep a notebook and a pen handy, especially if you're trying to collect achievements.

All in all, a fun game that's definitely worth a few bucks and a couple of hours.
